paragraphs: 1. By 2050, what percentage of our global population will live in cities?
d. The video does not say what percentage of our global population will live in cities.
2. What problem does Stuart Oda identify that is related to population density?
a. Oda reports that people waste far too much food.
b. Oda says that we must produce more food from less land and using fewer resources.
c. Oda says that we will not be able to produce enough food.
d. Oda identifies all of the above problems with population density.
3. Which of the following does Oda NOT cite as a problem facing society today?
a. Oda reports that 1/3 of all food is wasted.
b. Oda claims that 600 million people a year are sickened by bad food.
c. Oda says that agriculture accounts for 70% of all water use.
d. Oda says that that the rising price of agricultural production contributes to food shortages.
4. Why do people call indoor controlled farming “3-dimensional”?
a. It involves research, technology, and is climate controlled.
b. It eliminates pests, uses less water, and can be done almost anywhere.
c. Crops are grown in a 3-dimensional environment – length, breadth, and height.
d. Indoor farming makes use of time, temperature, and space.
5. Which of the following factors does Oda imply work against the popular acceptance of indoor agriculture?
a. The technology is fairly recent, and people don’t trust new technology.
b. Consumers remain concerned about where and how their food is grown.
c. The cost of controlled production is still higher than traditional agriculture.
d. All of the above are true and work against popular acceptance of indoor agriculture.
e. None of the above are true and they do not work against popular acceptance of indoor agriculture.
6. Which of the following are NOT essential to indoor agriculture?
a. Sunlight.
b. Racking systems.
c. Hydroponic materials.
d. All of the above are essential to indoor agriculture.
e. None of the above are essential to indoor agriculture.
7. Why is it important for indoor agricultural operations to use a precise nutrient formula for their plants?
a. Using a precise formula lowers costs.
b. Using a precise formula allows the operation to control or eliminate pests.
c. Using a precise formula grows healthier plants.
d. Using a precise formula allows the formula to be recycled.
8. Why might an indoor agricultural operation use sponges?
a. Oda says that sponges contain essential nutrients that promote healthy plant growth.
b. Oda says that sponges may be used in place of soil to grow plants.
c. Oda says that sponges are used to clean the lights, racks, and equipment.
d. Oda says that sponges are useful for stacking the plant racks.
9. Which of the following is NOT currently a benefit of indoor agriculture?
a. Indoor operations produce food of consistent quality.
b. Indoor operations can easily plan how much of a product to produce.
c. Indoor operations produce food all year.
d. Indoor operations can be located almost anywhere.
e. Indoor operations are cost efficient when compared to traditional agriculture.
f. All of the above currently benefits of indoor agriculture.
10. What are hydroponic materials?
a. Hydroponic materials produce artificial sunlight.
b. Hydroponic materials function as artificial soil for plants.
c. Hydroponic materials deliver and recycle water to the plants.
d. Hydroponic materials protect plants from pests and disease.
11. How does production per square meter in indoor agricultural operations compare to the production per
square meter of traditional farming?
a. Traditional farming produces more food per square meter than indoor agriculture.
b. Indoor agriculture and traditional farming produce about the same amount of food per meter squared.
c. Indoor agriculture produces much more food per square meter than traditional farming.
d. The video does not say which style of agriculture produces more food per square meter.
12. Oda cites three drawbacks to indoor agriculture. What are they?
a. Indoor operations use a lot of energy, have an overall high cost, and produce only a few varieties of crops.
b. Indoor operations use more water, more fertilizer, and require land in the city.
c. Indoor operations require automation, artificial lighting, and are vulnerable to pests and diseases.
d. Indoor operations are labor intensive, must be located close to their markets, and produce food of low quality.
13. According to the video, why do many indoor agricultural operations use robots?
a. Robots do not introduce pests or contamination into the operation.
b. Robots are better able to withstand long-term exposure to lasers and LED lighting.
c. Robots cost less than employing human workers.
d. Robots and artificial intelligence are better at monitoring plant health.
14. What other problem does Oda say that indoor agriculture solves?
a. Oda says that indoor farming in the future will create a new market for lasers.
b. Oda says that indoor farming makes use of underutilized urban space.
c. Oda says that indoor farming will reduce energy use.
d. Oda says that indoor farming produces less waste than traditional farming.
15. What does Oda say that implies that indoor agriculture can help feed starving people today?
a. Oda says that indoor agriculture can be done anywhere, including inhospitable environments.
b. Oda says that the technology is quickly becoming affordable.
c. Oda claims that some indoor farms produce 350 times the quantity of food per square meter.
d. Oda states that indoor agriculture eliminates pests.
e. Oda cites all of the above and they all imply that indoor agriculture can feed starving people today.
f. Oda cites NONE of the above as implying that indoor agriculture can feed starving people today.
16. According to Stuart Oda, why might he have become interested in indoor agriculture?
a. He wanted to make sure that people everywhere have enough food to eat.
b. He believes that as technology advances, production costs will decrease and indoor agriculture will become
profitable.
c. He says that his family name means “small farm” in Japanese.
d. Oda finds the study of indoor agriculture challenging and humbling.
